title.text: St. Francis of Assisi Parish Church, General Trias

title_en.text: St. Francis of Assisi Parish Church, General Trias

tagline.text: The 1769 stone church in General Trias where the national anthem was rehearsed

location.label: Location
location.text: Gov. Ferrer Drive, Poblacion, General Trias, Cavite

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (the October 4 parish feast is also a good time)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (one stop on a half-day Cavite route)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,000 (day trip from Manila, transport and snacks included, per person)

children.text: St. Francis of Assisi Parish Church in General Trias was rebuilt in stone from 1769 and, after earthquakes and restorations, was declared a historic structure in 1992. Its attached convent is said to be where the music for the 1898 independence proclamation was rehearsed, and it now houses the Museo de San Francisco de Malabon.

General Trias is a city in southern Cavite that was formerly called San Francisco de Malabon. Its patron saint, which gave the town its name, is St. Francis of Assisi, and the parish church named after him stands beside the central plaza in the town center. Wikipedia describes it as the first Catholic parish in General Trias, and it now belongs to the Diocese of Imus. Locally it is sometimes called the "GenTri church" or simply the General Trias church.

The church's history goes back to the early Spanish colonial period. According to Wikipedia, when the Franciscans first built a church here, the area was a small visita (sub-parish) of Cavite Viejo (present-day Kawit); in 1624 it passed to the Jesuits of Cavite Puerto (present-day Cavite City), and on September 9, 1753 it became an independent parish. Some blog sources give 1611 as the year of the first church, but the Wikipedia text gives no year, so sources differ. What is certain is that construction of a new stone church began in 1769, and the records say the work was led by Doña Maria Josepha de Yrizzari y Ursula, Countess of Lizarraga.

The church was repaired many times in the 19th century. It was repaired and enlarged in 1834; after the July 1880 Luzon earthquakes partly damaged it, the façade was rebuilt in 1881. It was refurbished again in 1885, its tiled roof was replaced with lighter galvanized iron in 1892 as protection against earthquakes, and it was repaired and enlarged once more in 1893. In the late 20th century it was restored close to its former appearance between 1989 and 1991, and it was reconsecrated on June 22, 1991 by Bishop Felix Perez of the Diocese of Imus. In 1992 the National Historical Institute (now the NHCP) declared it a historic structure and installed a marker.

What makes this church special is not only the building but its tie to the story of Philippine independence. The attached convent (convento) is said to be where the Banda San Francisco de Malabon rehearsed the "Marcha Filipina", the original piece behind today's national anthem, before it was played at the independence proclamation in Kawit on June 12, 1898. The convent building now houses the Museo de San Francisco de Malabon. For anyone following Cavite's historic sites, it pairs nicely with the Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit.

The façade is in the style often called "Earthquake Baroque," marked by tassel-like plaster moldings, large corbelled arches, and balustrade ornaments. This is the façade rebuilt in 1881, after the 1880 earthquake. Look first at the rounded arch of the entrance and the statue niches on either side.

blocks.title: Hexagonal bell tower and rose window

children.text: On the right stands a four-storey hexagonal bell tower that tapers as it rises, and above the entrance is a Gothic-style stained glass rose window. The open windows and balusters of the tower have a clear outline even from a distance, which makes the plaza a good spot for photos.

blocks.title: A spacious church about 55 m long

children.text: The church is described as about
long and
wide, with a nave about
wide. It is a barn-type structure with Baroque decoration added, and buttresses run along the sides. The first thing you notice inside is the wide, high sense of space.

The ceiling has a painting of the Pentecost, and the large altar enshrines a replica of the image of Our Lady of Solitude of Porta Vaga in Cavite City. The altar design is said to resemble that of Silang Church, so comparing the two can be fun.

blocks.title: Museo de San Francisco de Malabon

children.text: The convent next to the church is used as a museum. As a place tied to the story of the Marcha Filipina rehearsals, it is the church's biggest attraction. However, opening hours and admission terms differ between sources or could not be confirmed, so ask the parish before you visit.

A marker was installed in 1992 when the National Historical Institute declared the church a historic structure. Its text briefly summarizes the church's history and the 1898 story, which helps you get your bearings on site.

blocks.title: St. Francis statue carved from an acacia tree

children.text: One travel blog reports a wooden statue of St. Francis beside the church, made from the trunk of a century-old acacia tree that Typhoon Milenyo felled in 2006. Look for it as you walk around the plaza.

blocks.title: The town plaza next to the church

children.text: The church stands right beside the General Trias town plaza, so after your visit you can stroll around the plaza and get a glimpse of local life. The plaza tends to be crowded on weekends and on the parish feast day.
Get off on Gov. Ferrer Drive and walk toward the plaza where the church front is visible, taking in the whole façade and bell tower first.
Look closely at the arch, niches and rose window of the façade, and read the text on the NHCP marker.
If no Mass is under way, step quietly inside and admire the Pentecost painting on the ceiling and Our Lady of Solitude at the altar.
Check whether the museum in the neighboring convent is open, and if it is, look at the exhibits on the Marcha Filipina.
See the wooden statue of St. Francis beside the plaza, then have a snack or early lunch at a nearby eatery.
The church is still an active parish, so during Mass, worship takes priority over sightseeing. It helps to check the parish announcements before you go.
Leave Manila and head to Kawit along the Cavite coastal road or expressway.
Tour the Aguinaldo Shrine and meet the story of the 1898 independence proclamation first.
Move on to General Trias and continue with the story of the anthem rehearsals of that same year at St. Francis Church.
Have lunch in town and make a loop around the plaza and the church.
If time remains, head to other sites in Imus or Cavite City, or go home.
The trip from Kawit to General Trias can take quite a while depending on traffic, so it is best to leave in the morning.
The usual way is to take a Cavite-bound bus or UV Express from Metro Manila toward Dasmariñas or Imus, then transfer to a jeepney bound for General Trias.
Route-planning services give roughly
1–2 hours
from Manila to General Trias and about

by bus, but the figures differ very widely between sources (from around ₱100 up to ₱390) and some information is out of date. Under the March 2026 fare revision, a provincial aircon bus is about ₱2.45 per km and a traditional jeepney is ₱14 for the first km plus ₱2.00 per km.
The drop-off is in the town center along Gov. Ferrer Drive. Tell the conductor you want to get off at the "General Trias church" or in front of the "plaza."
Bus and jeepney routes and fares change often and an official route table could not be confirmed, so check locally.

items.title: From Manila by car or Grab

children.text: Sources give the distance from Manila to General Trias anywhere from about
35km
to
50km
. One source suggests about 1 hour 30 minutes by car.
The route combines the Cavite-bound expressway (CAVITEX and others) with local roads, and the travel time grows greatly during rush hours.
Grab or a rental car is convenient, but prices vary greatly with time of day and demand, so check the price shown in the app.
The church is right beside the town plaza, so once you reach the town center it is within walking distance.
From nearby barangays you can take a tricycle or jeepney; fares depend on the distance, so ask before you board.

In the dry season from November to May there is little worry about rain, so it is a good time to walk around the plaza and the church exterior. From March to May daytime temperatures are high and the sun is strong, so it is easier to go early in the morning.

October 4 is introduced as the feast of St. Francis, and the parish is liveliest then. However, the crowds make quiet sightseeing difficult, and event schedules can change from year to year, so check the parish announcements. Mass schedules also differ from usual during Holy Week and Christmas.

General Trias has some small guesthouses and eateries in the town center, but not many lodging choices like a tourist city. If you plan to see only the church, the museum, and the town plaza, many visitors make it a day trip from Manila.

For meals, a local eatery or snack stall around the plaza is a light, easy choice. For Cavite local food, it is easiest to look and choose at a restaurant in town. If you want to stay overnight, compare lodging in Imus or Tagaytay in Cavite as well.
The church is still an active Catholic parish. Avoid photography and loud talking during Mass.
Sleeveless tops and short shorts may be a problem for entry, so covering your shoulders and knees is recommended.
Since whether the museum is open is uncertain, contact the parish Facebook page or office (the number listed is (046) 437-7339) before you go.
Early morning is coolest and the area in front of the church is quiet, which is good for photos.
Combining it with the Aguinaldo Shrine in Kawit on the same day carries the 1898 independence story through.
Mass schedules differ between sources, so check the latest announcement if you visit on a Sunday.
The museum's opening hours and admission terms could not be confirmed from an official source, so be sure to ask the parish before you visit.
Public transport routes and fares differ between information services and include outdated information, so check again locally.
The year the church was first built (the 1611 account) is stated differently in different sources.
Sightseeing access may be restricted during Mass.
Cavite roads are very congested at rush hours, so allow plenty of travel time.
Follow on-site notices on whether photography is allowed inside the church and museum.
